passages.title: Twelve Cookies
sentences: Grandma Rose gave Sam twelve cookies.
"Share them with your friends," she said.
Sam sat on the steps with Priya, Leo and Maya.
He gave each friend three cookies.
He kept three for himself.
Leo counted his cookies.
Then he counted Sam's.
"We all have the same," Leo said. "That is fair."

passages.title: Turns on the Big Ramp
sentences: On Sunday, the big ramp at the skate park was busy.
Some older kids took turn after turn.
A small boy named Jai stood by the side with his board.
He waited and waited.
Leo saw him and had an idea.
He took a marker and a piece of cardboard out of his bag.
"Let's make a list," he said. "Each person gets one turn, then goes to the back."
He wrote every name on the list, and Jai's name went on too.
The older kids grumbled at first.
Then they saw that everyone got lots of turns.
When Jai rolled down the ramp, the whole line cheered.

passages.title: The Fox and the Stork
sentences: One day, a fox asked a stork to come for dinner.
The fox served soup in a wide, flat dish.
He lapped up his soup fast.
The stork had a long, thin beak.
Her beak tapped the flat dish, but she got only a few drops.
The fox grinned at her.
The next week, the stork asked the fox to dinner.
She served soup in a tall jar with a narrow neck.
The stork dipped her long beak in and drank it all.
The fox could only lick the outside of the jar.
He went home hungry.
"Now you know how it feels," said the stork.

passages.title: The Honest Woodcutter
sentences: A poor woodcutter was chopping a tree beside a deep river.
His axe slipped out of his hands and fell into the water with a splash.
It was his only axe, and he needed it for his work.
He sat on the bank and put his head in his hands.
Then a river spirit rose up out of the water.
She held up an axe made of shining gold.
"Is this your axe?" she asked.
"That axe is gold," said the woodcutter. "My axe is plain iron."
Next, the spirit held up a silver axe.
"My axe is plain iron," he said again.
At last, she held up his old iron axe.
"Yes, that one is mine!" he said, and he smiled.
The spirit was pleased that he told the truth.
She gave him all three axes to take home.

passages.title: The Broken Mug
sentences: After school, Leo and Sam stopped at the Lighthouse Café for hot chocolate.
Leo had his skateboard under his arm.
As he turned to sit down, the end of the board hit a mug on the shelf.
The mug fell to the floor and broke into three pieces.
The café was busy, and the owner, Mrs. Lin, was in the back.
Leo's face went red.
He picked up the pieces and walked to the counter.
"Mrs. Lin, I broke one of your mugs with my board," he said. "I am sorry."
He took four dollars from his pocket.
"I can pay for it," he said.
Mrs. Lin looked at the pieces and then at Leo.
"Thank you for telling me," she said. "That was honest."
"Keep your money. Next time, carry your board by the wheels."

items.hint: Count how many cookies each friend got. Then count how many Sam kept.
items.explain: The sharing was fair because everyone got the same number. Each friend got three, and Sam kept three. Leo says, "We all have the same."

items.prompt: Sort these ways to share the cookies. Is each one fair?

cards.text: Sam keeps six cookies for himself.
Sam saves three cookies for a friend who is late.
Leo takes the cookies from Maya.

items.hint: Ask: does each friend end up with the same? If yes, it is fair.
items.explain: Fair: each friend gets three, and saving three for a late friend. Not fair: Sam keeping six, and Leo taking Maya's cookies. In the story, Sam gave everyone three.

items.prompt: What did Leo do to make the ramp fair?
options: He made a list so each person got a turn.
He let his friends go first.
He kept the ramp for himself.
items.hint: Find the part where Leo has an idea. Read what he says and writes.
items.explain: Leo made a list so each person got one turn and then went to the back. He wrote every name on it, and Jai's name too.

items.prompt: Sort what can happen at the ramp. Is each one fair?

cards.text: Each person gets one turn, then goes to the back.
A few kids take turn after turn.
Leo writes every name on the list.
A big kid cuts to the front of the line.
Jai's name goes on the list too.

items.hint: Fair turns mean every person gets a chance. Ask: does each person get a chance?
items.explain: Fair: one turn each, every name on the list, and Jai on the list too. Not fair: a few kids taking turn after turn, and cutting to the front. Leo's list fixed the problem in the story.

items.prompt: Was Leo's list a good idea? Build your answer.

items.explain: One good answer is: I think Leo's list was fair because every kid got a turn. Any honest answer is fine.

items.prompt: Why was the fox's dinner unkind to the stork?
options: The flat dish was wrong for her long beak.
items.hint: Look at the dish the fox used. Then look at the shape of the stork's beak.
items.explain: The flat dish was wrong for the stork's long, thin beak. She got only a few drops. This is in the first five sentences.

items.prompt: The stork played the same trick back on the fox. Was that fair? Build your answer.

slots.label: Reason

now the fox knows how it feels
both of them went home hungry

items.explain: One good answer is: I think the stork's trick was fair because the fox did it to her first. Another person might say a good friend forgives. Any honest answer is fine.

items.prompt: The spirit held up a gold axe. Why did the woodcutter say his axe was plain iron?
options: He wanted to tell the truth.
He liked silver more than gold.
The gold axe was too heavy.
He was angry at the spirit.
items.hint: Read what the spirit thinks near the end. It tells you what kind of person the woodcutter is.
items.explain: He wanted to tell the truth. His real axe was plain iron. Near the end, the spirit is pleased that he told the truth.

items.prompt: Tap a sentence that shows the woodcutter was honest.
items.hint: Look for the times the woodcutter speaks. Check if he tells the truth about his axe.
items.explain: The woodcutter told the truth each time. He said, "My axe is plain iron," for the gold and the silver axes. He said, "Yes, that one is mine!" for his real axe.

items.prompt: What honest thing did Leo do?
options: He told Mrs. Lin that he broke the mug.
He hid the pieces under a table.
He said the mug fell by itself.
items.hint: Find what Leo says when he gets to the counter.
items.explain: Leo told Mrs. Lin that he broke the mug with his board. He said it at the counter, and he said sorry.

items.prompt: What do you think of what Leo did? Build your answer.

slots.label: More (you can skip this)
options: It can feel hard to tell the truth.

items.hint: Think about what Leo did after the mug broke. Which of those things do you think matters most?
items.explain: One good answer is: I think Leo was honest because he told the truth. Mrs. Lin said, "That was honest." Any honest answer is fine.

steps.say: Fair can mean everyone gets the same. So I count what each person got.
Sam gave each friend three cookies.
He kept three for himself. Three and three are the same.
Leo checked too. He said, "We all have the same."
So Sam's sharing was fair because everyone got the same number.
